title: Start a handheld 3D scanner with its button and scan a cast housing all round, up over its top, to compare with its CAD
instruction: Start scanning with button 4 on the back of the scanner's handle, scan the part on the turntable until the scan covers 95 % of its outer surface, its top included, then move the scanner and your hands at least 3 cm away from the part.
context: Inspectors, testers, sorters, samplers and weighers (O*NET 51-9061, 602,000 US workers) have the Core task "Inspect, test, or measure materials, products, installations, or work for conformance to specifications." The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook for them: "Although some still use hand-held measuring devices, such as calipers and alignment gauges, workers more commonly operate electronic inspection equipment, such as coordinate-measuring machines (CMMs) and three-dimensional (3D) scanners." Here a cast housing on a turntable is scanned all round with a handheld 3D scanner for comparison with its CAD, as foundries inspect castings. The scanner records only after its button is pressed, inside its range, facing the surface, moved slowly enough to keep tracking; the top needs views from above. In the demo one hand holds the scanner while the other presses its button, then turns the platter in strokes as the scanner climbs over the part's top. The task does not ask for two hands.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A manual turntable on a ball bearing, 30 cm across, is centred at (42, 0); its platter, 3 cm high with a rubber top and white ticks every 15 degrees, turns freely. On its centre stands a cast-iron plummer block housing, an SKF SY 505 M without its bearing insert (painted grey; a 127 x 38 mm base 16 mm thick with two bolt slots, the bore's axis 36.5 mm up, a 52 mm bore, 71 mm tall; 0.55 kg), its base's length along x; it is not fixed and rides round with the platter. A handheld 3D scanner, a Shining 3D EinScan H2 (108 x 110 x 237 mm, 731 g; working distance 200 to 700 mm, a field of view of up to 420 x 440 mm at 470 mm), stands on its head on the table at (20, -12), its handle up and its lens toward -y, away from the part. The scanning software is open in preview, so scanning is off until button 4 on the back of its handle (Preview / Scan / Pause, per the maker's quick start guide; shown in orange) is pressed. A 20 x 13 cm tablet on a stand at (62, -22) runs a simple scanning app, as the scanner's own software (Shining 3D's EXScan H) shows a scan: two live views, from either side and above, empty until scanning starts and showing only the surface captured so far, built up as it is scanned; a distance indicator, ten 7.5 cm cells (green from 22.5 to 67.5 cm, red outside) with a white mark at the scanner's distance from the part; a tracking badge (green while tracking, red when tracking is lost, grey when not scanning); and a coverage bar, one cell for each 10 %. It is a display; the score reads the poses. The arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: Real trial: the scan's mesh is compared with the housing's CAD in CloudCompare; coverage is the share of its surface within 1 mm of the scan, leaving out the underside and the insides of the bore and the bolt slots, as the simulation does; the top is the faces turned within 30 degrees of straight up. The software's log shows when scanning started and when tracking held. A camera above the station shows touches, drops, the part against its outline drawn on the platter, and the 3 cm clearance held 1 s. Simulation: 4,829 points on that surface, 1,007 on the top. Nothing counts until button 4 is pressed (a fingertip on its face); a second press pauses scanning, a third resumes it, and nothing counts while paused. A point counts when, while the scanner scans and tracks, it is in view (20 to 70 cm along the axis, about 48 x 50 degrees), faces the scanner within 45 degrees, and is not hidden by the part or the platter. Tracking: relative motion under 0.25 m/s and 60 degrees/s with a quarter of the part's points in view; once lost after scanning began, it returns only on a view of 50 points, 30 % of them already scanned. 1.0 once 95 % is covered, with every fingertip of both grippers and the scanner 3 cm or more from the part, held 1 s; the trial then ends. Otherwise, at the end: 0.5 at 70 % with half the top, 0.25 at 40 %, else 0. 0 at any time if the part moves 2 cm off centre or tips 15 degrees, the scanner comes within 2 mm of the part or the turntable, a fingertip within 2 mm of the part, or the scanner, not held by its handle, falls faster than 0.8 m/s.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at 240 Hz on GPU. The scanner is a free body of the EinScan H2's size and mass, head and handle as boxes, with no cable. Button 4 is coded: a fingertip pressed on it starts scanning, a second press pauses it. The scan is not rendered: coverage is geometry over sampled surface points, using the maker's working distance and field of view. The 45 degree facing limit and the tracking rules are assumptions, to measure. The arms do not block the scanner's view in the count.
